headline: Gemini 4 has another new flavor: Neon
summary: Only one thing worth a look today: Google released Gemini 4 Neon, and the pricing is a bit of a mess.

items.title: Gemini 4 Neon is out
actions: Developers can pick Neon in the Gemini API, Google AI Studio, and Google Antigravity
I couldn't find any official word on Neon in the regular Gemini app yet. Check "Introducing Gemini 4 Neon" on blog.google
deep_dive: Price: according to OpenRouter, Neon costs $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. Carbon's discounted price is $2/$10, going up to $4/$20 after December 1.
Simon Willison thinks pricing across the Gemini 4 lineup was already confusing, and Neon makes it worse. He released llm-gemini 0.38 to support Neon.
"3x faster than Carbon with similar quality" is Google's own claim. The independent tests I've seen disagree with each other, and nothing's been confirmed yet.
items.signals: HN 867 points · 686 comments · Simon Willison hands-on test · Josh Woodward announced it
items.what: Gemini 4 Neon is a new AI model Google released on November 18. It's the middle tier of the Gemini 4 lineup. Carbon is saved for the hardest long tasks, Hydrogen is the faster everyday option, and Neon sits between the two. Google says it finishes tasks about 3 times faster than Carbon with similar quality, and it's better at understanding complicated instructions.
items.meaning: Google now has one more option that's all about speed and value. Since you use Claude Code and codex day to day, there's no need to switch any time soon.

items.title: Putting agents in an external sandbox
items.signals: Published by Simon Willison on Nov 17 · Done with Prime Radiant · Three sandbox implementations
items.what: This is an experimental setup that Simon Willison and Prime Radiant put out around November 17, called an "external sandbox" (a safe little room kept separate from your computer). The AI coding assistant itself stays outside, and the commands it wants to run go into a Linux sandbox instead. It works with tools like Claude Code and Codex, has the network turned off by default, and can only touch the mounted folders and allowed URLs.
items.meaning: Even if the AI's code goes wrong or it gets tricked by a malicious prompt, it's harder for it to hurt your computer. But it's experimental and mostly aimed at developers for now.
actions: If you want to try it, first read the external-sandboxes-for-coding-agents post on simonwillison.net (2026/Nov/17), then follow its links to find Prime Radiant's implementation
deep_dive: Known gap: Claude Code only sends Bash commands into the sandbox. Its built-in file reading and editing still run on your computer. Codex and Pi send more operations into the sandbox.
Prime Radiant says these implementations are experimental prototypes that haven't been audited enough, so they're not suitable for sensitive stuff.
These details come from a secondhand article, and I didn't get to read Prime Radiant's original. Please double-check before you use it.
